claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been produced in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Incorporating hierarchical-microstructure descriptors into an active multi-fidelity machine-learning framework will improve predictions of Young’s modulus for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will improve predictions of yield strength for HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will improve predictions of fracture toughness for HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate model will use phase or domain size distributions, interface characteristics, interfacial area densities, and local compositional gradients as input features.
Active learning will prioritize high-fidelity phase-field or mesoscale finite-element simulations in regions where model uncertainty is high.

Characteristic phase or domain sizes, interfacial area densities, and local compositional gradients mediate the relationship between hierarchical microstructure and macroscopic mechanical performance.
Explicit hierarchical-microstructure features enable the surrogate model to capture mechanical-property dependence on local structure better than global thermophysical and compositional inputs alone.
Concentrating high-fidelity calculations in high-uncertainty regions reduces the total computational demand.
The proposed method will reduce calculation time by approximately a factor of 10 relative to traditional thermophysical, CALPHAD, first-principles, and global-descriptor modeling methods.
The proposed method will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 15–20% relative to traditional methods.
The framework is intended to operate from room temperature to approximately 400–600 °C when strain rates and loading conditions match the calibration experiments.
The framework will become unreliable at temperatures or strain rates that produce untrained microstructural changes such as phase coarsening or altered heterogeneity.
The framework may become unreliable when the processed material deviates from the reported hierarchical heterostructure.
Preliminary tests suggest gains in predictive accuracy and computational efficiency.
The hypothesis will be falsified if more than 10% of predictions differ by more than ±10% from measured values for any of Young’s modulus, yield strength, or fracture toughness.
